```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  dpi = 96
)
has_gdal <- requireNamespace("gdalraster", quietly = TRUE)
has_ximage <- requireNamespace("ximage", quietly = TRUE)
```

shallows solves the two-dimensional shallow water (Saint-Venant) equations
on a regular grid: the same grid as a raster DEM. This vignette goes through
the model, how to set up and run it, how to read what comes back, and how
far the results can be trusted, with each claim checked by a small run you
can repeat.

```{r setup}
library(shallows)
```

## The model

The unknowns are depth $h$ and momentum $(hu, hv)$ on each cell, over a
bed $z$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
h_t + (hu)_x + (hv)_y &= R \\
(hu)_t + \left(hu^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} g h^2\right)_x + (huv)_y &= -g h z_x - g n^2 u |\mathbf{u}| / h^{1/3} + f\,hv \\
(hv)_t + (huv)_x + \left(hv^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} g h^2\right)_y &= -g h z_y - g n^2 v |\mathbf{u}| / h^{1/3} - f\,hu
\end{aligned}
$$

with rain $R$ (m/s), Manning roughness $n$ and Coriolis parameter
$f$. The scheme is a finite volume method with the HLL Riemann solver
and the hydrostatic reconstruction of Audusse et al. (2004). That
reconstruction gives the two properties that matter most on real terrain:

* **Well balanced.** Water at rest over any bed stays at rest to round-off,
  so the bed slope term never invents currents.
* **Positive.** Depth never goes negative under the time step limit, so
  cells wet and dry with no special cases.

`order = 1` is piecewise constant in space with forward Euler in time.
`order = 2` (the default) adds MUSCL reconstruction with the minmod limiter
and Heun's method (SSP-RK2) in time. Friction is semi-implicit, rotation is
applied exactly in Strang half steps, and the time step comes from the CFL
condition. The kernel is about 400 lines of C++ in `src/swe.cpp`, with
OpenMP over the flux sweeps.

## A state and a run

A simulation needs a state, made by `sw_state()`, and output times given to
`sw_run()`. Matrices are oriented like a raster: row 1 is the north edge,
column 1 the west edge, `hu` is eastward momentum and `hv` is momentum
towards increasing row number (southward on a north-up grid).

Plots here use [ximage](https://github.com/hypertidy/ximage), which
draws a matrix in that same raster order, placed by an extent given as
`c(xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)`; a state built from a DEM carries its extent
in the same form.

Here is a 2 m hump of water in the middle of a flat 1 m deep pool, 10 m
cells, with walls on every edge:

```{r first-run}
n <- 81; dx <- 10
xy <- (seq_len(n) - (n + 1) / 2) * dx
r2 <- outer(xy^2, xy^2, "+")
s <- sw_state(z = matrix(0, n, n), h = 1 + 2 * exp(-r2 / 50^2), dx = dx)
run <- sw_run(s, times = c(10, 20, 40))
run
```

The result holds one depth and momentum matrix per output time, and a
diagnostics table:

```{r first-run-diag}
str(run$h, max.level = 1)
run$diag
```

| column | meaning |
|---|---|
| `volume` | water on the grid (m^3) |
| `outflow`, `rain` | cumulative volume out through open edges, and in as rain |
| `steps`, `dt_min`, `dt_max` | cumulative time steps and the range of stable steps |
| `clipped` | volume removed by clipping negative depths (should be 0) |
| `budget_error` | `volume - (initial + rain - outflow)` |

The budget is the first thing to look at after any run: it should close to
round-off, and here it does.

```{r first-run-plot, eval = has_ximage, fig.height = 3, fig.alt = "Three depth maps at 10, 20 and 40 seconds showing a circular wave spreading from a central hump of water."}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
for (k in 1:3) {
  ximage::ximage(run$h[[k]], extent = c(0, n * dx, 0, n * dx), zlim = c(0.4, 1.6),
                 col = hcl.colors(96, "viridis"), asp = 1, axes = FALSE,
                 main = sprintf("t = %g s", run$diag$time[k]))
}
par(op)
```

## Dam breaks: shocks and rarefactions

A dam break along one row of cells has an exact solution. With water
downstream (Stoker) the solution is a rarefaction, a constant middle state
and a shock; onto a dry bed (Ritter) the front is a wet/dry edge. A one-row
grid with open ends is enough:

```{r dambreak, fig.alt = "Depth profiles for Stoker and Ritter dam breaks after 20 seconds: exact solution with first and second order model results."}
dam <- function(nx, order, hr) {
  dx <- 1000 / nx
  x <- -500 + (seq_len(nx) - 0.5) * dx
  s <- sw_state(matrix(0, 1, nx), h = matrix(ifelse(x < 0, 10, hr), 1, nx), dx = dx)
  r <- sw_run(s, times = 20, order = order, bc = "open")
  list(x = x, h = r$h[[1]][1, ])
}
x <- -500 + (seq_len(200) - 0.5) * 5
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 2, 1))
for (hr in c(2, 0)) {
  ex <- if (hr > 0) dambreak_stoker(x, 20, 10, hr) else dambreak_ritter(x, 20, 10)
  plot(ex$x, ex$h, type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "x (m)", ylab = "depth (m)",
       main = if (hr > 0) "Stoker (wet bed)" else "Ritter (dry bed)")
  lines(x, dam(200, 1, hr)$h, col = "darkorange")
  lines(x, dam(200, 2, hr)$h, col = "steelblue", lty = 2)
  legend("topright", c("exact", "order 1", "order 2"), bty = "n",
         col = c("black", "darkorange", "steelblue"), lty = c(1, 1, 2))
}
par(op)
```

Refining the grid shows how the error falls. Near a shock no scheme does
better than first order, so the gain from `order = 2` is a smaller constant
rather than a faster rate:

```{r dambreak-convergence}
conv <- expand.grid(nx = c(100, 200, 400, 800), order = 1:2)
conv$L1 <- mapply(function(nx, o) {
  d <- dam(nx, o, 2)
  mean(abs(d$h - dambreak_stoker(d$x, 20, 10, 2)$h))
}, conv$nx, conv$order)
xtabs(L1 ~ nx + order, conv)
```

## Lake at rest

A well-balanced scheme keeps still water still over any bed, including
where islands stick out of it. A rough bed with two hills and a level of
0.5 m:

```{r lake}
n <- 60
ij <- expand.grid(i = 1:n, j = 1:n)
set.seed(4417)
z <- matrix(0.6 * exp(-((ij$i - 20)^2 + (ij$j - 25)^2) / 40) +
            0.8 * exp(-((ij$i - 40)^2 + (ij$j - 40)^2) / 90) +
            0.05 * runif(n * n), n, n)
r <- sw_run(sw_state(z, eta = 0.5), times = 100)
wet <- r$h[[1]] > 0
c(dry_cells = sum(!wet),
  max_surface_error = max(abs(r$h[[1]][wet] + z[wet] - 0.5)),
  max_momentum = max(abs(c(r$hu[[1]], r$hv[[1]]))))
```

## Wetting and drying: Thacker's bowl

In a paraboloid bowl the water surface can stay a tilted plane that circles
around the bowl, so the shoreline moves across dry ground every period.
`thacker_bowl()` gives the exact bed, depth and velocity at any time; start
from its state at `t = 0` and compare after a full period:

```{r thacker}
P <- thacker_bowl(0, 0, 0)$period
n <- 80; dx <- 4 / n
x <- -2 + (seq_len(n) - 0.5) * dx
X <- matrix(x, n, n, byrow = TRUE); Y <- matrix(x, n, n)
a0 <- thacker_bowl(X, Y, 0)
s <- sw_state(a0$z, h = a0$h, hu = a0$h * a0$u, hv = a0$h * a0$v, dx = dx)
r <- sw_run(s, times = P * c(0.25, 0.5, 1))
rel_L1 <- sapply(1:3, function(k) sum(abs(r$h[[k]] - thacker_bowl(X, Y, r$diag$time[k])$h)) / sum(a0$h))
data.frame(time = r$diag$time / P, rel_L1, min_depth = sapply(r$h, min), clipped = r$diag$clipped)
```

A section through the centre (row `k0`) at each output time: the lines are
the exact surface, the dots are the model where it is wet.

```{r thacker-plot, fig.alt = "Section through the Thacker paraboloid bowl showing the tilted water surface at a quarter, half and full period, model dots on exact lines."}
k0 <- which.min(abs(x))
plot(x, a0$z[k0, ], type = "l", col = "grey40", lwd = 2, ylim = c(-0.1, 0.06),
     xlab = "x (m)", ylab = "elevation (m)")
cols <- c("darkorange", "steelblue", "firebrick")
for (k in 1:3) {
  ex <- thacker_bowl(x, x[k0], r$diag$time[k])
  w <- ex$h > 0
  lines(x[w], (ex$h + ex$z)[w], col = cols[k], lwd = 2)
  h <- r$h[[k]][k0, ]; w <- h > 1e-4
  points(x[w], (h + a0$z[k0, ])[w], col = cols[k], pch = 20, cex = 0.6)
}
legend("top", c("T/4", "T/2", "T"), col = cols, lwd = 2, bty = "n", horiz = TRUE)
```

## Rain, friction, open edges and the budget

Rain is a source term (m/s, a scalar or a matrix), Manning `n` is the
friction, and each edge can be `"wall"`, `"open"` or `"periodic"`, given as
one value or by name. Here 50 mm/h falls for 10 minutes on a generated
valley with fractal roughness that drains out of its open east edge, then
`sw_continue()` picks up from the last frame with the rain turned off:

```{r rain}
z <- sw_generate("valley", nx = 120, ny = 60, dx = 5,
                 noise = list(amp = 0.5, seed = 2207), as = "matrix")
s <- sw_state(z, dx = 5, manning = 0.04, rain = 50 / 1000 / 3600)
bc <- c(west = "wall", east = "open", north = "wall", south = "wall")
wet <- sw_run(s, times = seq(60, 600, by = 60), bc = bc)
dry <- sw_run(sw_continue(wet, rain = 0), times = seq(60, 600, by = 60), bc = bc)
wet
dry
```

The two phases join into one water budget: rain in, water stored on the
valley, and water out through the east edge.

```{r rain-budget, fig.alt = "Water budget over 20 minutes: cumulative rain, volume stored in the valley, and cumulative outflow through the east edge."}
d <- rbind(wet$diag,
           transform(dry$diag, time = time + 600,
                     rain = rain + wet$diag$rain[10],
                     outflow = outflow + wet$diag$outflow[10]))
plot(d$time / 60, d$rain, type = "l", lty = 2, ylim = c(0, max(d$rain)),
     xlab = "minutes", ylab = expression(m^3))
lines(d$time / 60, d$volume, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
lines(d$time / 60, d$outflow, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", c("rain in", "stored", "out through the east edge"), bty = "n",
       lty = c(2, 1, 1), col = c("black", "steelblue", "firebrick"))
```

Depth when the rain stops, over the bed in grey (cells shallower than 1 mm
left out):

```{r rain-depth, eval = has_ximage, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Map of water depth along the valley floor when the rain stops, over the grey bed."}
ext <- c(0, 120 * 5, 0, 60 * 5)
h <- wet$h[[10]]
h[h < 0.001] <- NA
ximage::ximage(z, extent = ext, col = grey.colors(96), asp = 1,
               xlab = "x (m)", ylab = "y (m)")
ximage::ximage(h, extent = ext, col = hcl.colors(96, "Blues 3", rev = TRUE), add = TRUE)
```

## Earth rotation

`sw_state(f = )` takes a Coriolis parameter, and `sw_coriolis()` gives it
from a latitude (or per cell from a state or grid with a CRS). With no
pressure gradient, a uniform current should turn in a circle at the
inertial period $2\pi / |f|$ without losing speed: anticlockwise in the
southern hemisphere. A doubly periodic flat basin at 43 S, starting with
1 m/s eastward:

```{r inertial, fig.alt = "Hodograph of velocity over one inertial period: a unit circle traced anticlockwise from eastward flow."}
f <- sw_coriolis(-43)
Tin <- 2 * pi / abs(f)
s <- sw_state(matrix(0, 4, 4), h = 10, hu = 10, dx = 10000, f = f)
r <- sw_run(s, times = Tin * seq(0.05, 1, by = 0.05), bc = "periodic")
u <- sapply(r$hu, `[`, 1) / 10
v <- -sapply(r$hv, `[`, 1) / 10  # hv points south; flip to northward
c(inertial_period_h = Tin / 3600, speed_range = range(sqrt(u^2 + v^2)))
plot(c(1, u), c(0, v), type = "b", asp = 1, pch = 20,
     xlab = "u, eastward (m/s)", ylab = "v, northward (m/s)")
arrows(1, 0, u[2], v[2], col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, length = 0.1)
```

The first steps (arrow) go from eastward towards northward: anticlockwise,
as expected south of the equator.

## Rasters in and out

Raster input and output go through GDAL with
[gdalraster](https://github.com/firelab/gdalraster). Grids use the layout
of `gdalraster::read_ds()`: cell values in raster order (row major, top
row first) with a `gis` attribute holding the extent, dimensions and CRS.
`ximage::ximage()` plots such a grid directly, in place, and `sw_matrix()`
turns one into a matrix.

* `sw_from_rast()` builds a state from a grid, a file or GDAL source name,
  or an open `gdalraster::GDALRaster`, keeping the extent and CRS.
* `sw_generate()` returns a grid in local metres (no CRS).
* `sw_frames()` turns a run into one grid per output time: depth, surface
  elevation, speed or momentum.
* `sw_write()` writes those frames to a multi-band GeoTIFF.

A reservoir with a dam breached over 20 m, filled to 14 m behind the dam:

```{r reservoir, eval = has_ximage, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Three maps of flow speed after a reservoir dam breach at 20, 60 and 120 seconds."}
bed <- sw_generate("reservoir", nx = 300, ny = 80, dx = 5, breach = 20)
# fill behind the intact dam, then run on the breached bed
lake <- sw_fill_lake(sw_generate("reservoir", nx = 300, ny = 80, dx = 5),
                     i0 = 40, j0 = 100, level = 14)
s <- sw_from_rast(bed, h = lake, manning = 0.03)
r <- sw_run(s, times = c(20, 60, 120), bc = "open")
r
sp <- sw_frames(r, "speed")
# ximage leaves values outside zlim transparent, so cover the full range
zl <- c(0, max(unlist(sp), na.rm = TRUE))
zl
op <- par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
for (fr in sp) {
  ximage::ximage(bed, col = grey.colors(96), asp = 1, axes = FALSE,
                 main = sprintf("speed over the bed, t = %g s", attr(fr, "time")))
  ximage::ximage(fr, zlim = zl, col = hcl.colors(96, "Inferno"), add = TRUE)
}
par(op)
```

Writing the frames is then one call, and the file reads back with any
GDAL tool:

```{r write, eval = has_gdal}
f <- tempfile(fileext = ".tif")
sw_write(r, f, "h")
ds <- new(gdalraster::GDALRaster, f)
c(bands = ds$getRasterCount(), band_3 = ds$getDescription(3))
ds$close()
```

For a real place, `sw_extract()` reads a bed straight from cloud
optimised GeoTIFFs (the Tasmania 2 m DEM, Copernicus GLO-30 and GEBCO,
finest first) into a local metre grid. It needs a network connection, so
it is not run here:

```{r extract, eval = FALSE}
bed <- sw_extract(147.45, -43.05, size = 40000, res = 200)  # Storm Bay
s <- sw_from_rast(bed, eta = 0)
```

`inst/examples/mcrobies-storm.R` is a complete worked case: a 40 minute
storm over a 1.2 km tile of real terrain, written out as GeoTIFFs with a
budget.

## A readable reference implementation

`sw_run_r()` is the first-order scheme written in plain vectorised R. It
is slow, but it is the clearest description of what the C++ does, and the
two agree to round-off:

```{r reference}
n <- 25
ij <- expand.grid(i = 1:n, j = 1:n)
z <- matrix(0.3 * exp(-((ij$i - 10)^2 + (ij$j - 12)^2) / 20), n, n)
s <- sw_state(z, eta = 0.4)
s$h[5:8, 5:8] <- s$h[5:8, 5:8] + 0.2
a <- sw_run(s, times = 4, order = 1, bc = "open")
b <- sw_run_r(s, times = 4, bc = "open")
max(abs(a$h[[1]] - b$h[[1]]))
```

## Limits

* The grid is Cartesian in a projected CRS. Coriolis is included, but
  ocean-basin scales would also need spherical metric terms.
* Time stepping is explicit, so the step is set by the fastest and deepest
  water: halving the cell size costs about eight times as much per
  simulated minute.
* There is no infiltration, no inflow hydrograph boundary, and roughness
  is whatever Manning matrix you supply. There are no drains or culverts,
  so on real terrain water ponds behind road fill.
* Results on real terrain are for illustration, not engineering or
  planning.

## References

* Audusse, E., Bouchut, F., Bristeau, M.-O., Klein, R. and Perthame, B.
  (2004). A fast and stable well-balanced scheme with hydrostatic
  reconstruction for shallow water flows. *SIAM J. Sci. Comput.* 25,
  2050-2065.
* Kurganov, A. and Petrova, G. (2007). A second-order well-balanced
  positivity preserving central-upwind scheme for the Saint-Venant
  system. *Commun. Math. Sci.* 5, 133-160.
* Thacker, W. C. (1981). Some exact solutions to the nonlinear
  shallow-water wave equations. *J. Fluid Mech.* 107, 499-508.
* Delestre, O. et al. (2013). SWASHES: a compilation of shallow water
  analytic solutions for hydraulic and environmental studies. *Int. J.
  Numer. Meth. Fluids* 72, 269-300.
